analysis.one_liner: Orders federal banking regulators to study how bank-fintech partnerships affect the banking sector and consumers.
analysis.headline: The Senate bill to study bank-fintech partnerships was referred to the Banking Committee on June 18, 2026, and has seen no action since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill directs three federal banking regulators — the Federal Reserve, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, and the FDIC — to study how partnerships between banks and financial technology companies affect competition, innovation, consumer protection, and access to financial products, and to recommend any changes to laws or rules that would promote such partnerships. The National Credit Union Administration would run a parallel study for credit unions. Each regulator would report its findings to Congress within one year. The bill itself changes no rules; it only commissions research.
analysis.who_benefits: If enacted, the main beneficiaries would be the financial technology industry and banks seeking regulatory changes that make bank-fintech partnerships easier — for example, lower compliance burdens and faster product rollouts, which could eventually mean more convenient and possibly cheaper financial products for consumers. Community banks and credit unions could also gain tools to compete digitally. But the bill mandates only a study, so no one benefits materially unless later legislation follows.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Federal Reserve, the Comptroller of the Currency, and the FDIC to study how bank-fintech partnerships affect competition, innovation, consumer protection, new bank formation, and compliance burdens, and to recommend legal or regulatory changes that would promote such partnerships.
Requires the National Credit Union Administration to run a parallel study on credit union-fintech partnerships and report findings to Congress within one year of enactment.

analysis.who_pays: No one bears a direct cost; the bill spends no money beyond the agencies' staff time to conduct the studies. The potential longer-term cost falls on consumers if regulators adopt recommendations that loosen consumer protections around fintech-bank arrangements.

drawbacks.text: A study alone changes nothing: banking agencies already examine bank-fintech partnerships, so the bill spends regulatory time and produces a report with no binding effect on rules or consumer protections.

The study's framing directs the agencies toward finding ways to 'promote' partnerships, which could lay groundwork for loosening oversight of fintech companies that have been associated with consumer complaints and bank failures when fintech programs at partner banks have failed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost is minimal — a required study and report. But the benefit is also speculative: the bill presupposes that bank-fintech partnerships should be promoted, so the study may frame the issue in the industry's favor, and any later rule changes built on it could matter far more than the study itself. As written, it is low-impact either way.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, and no committee or floor action has followed.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 18, 2026 and read twice before being referred to the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee.
No markup, hearing, vote, or further action has been recorded since the referral.
It has one Democratic cosponsor alongside Republican sponsor Pete Ricketts.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nobody has materially gained or lost yet; the bill sits in committee. If it never advances, the status quo remains, which banks and fintech companies with established regulator relationships can navigate better than newcomers.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; bill sits in committee

for.name: Sen. Pete Ricketts
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and had it referred to the Senate Banking Committee.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Republican senator with one Democratic cosponsor, so support crosses party lines but is very thin: two senators out of 100.

industries.note: The study is explicitly designed to identify ways to promote bank-fintech partnerships, potentially easing the path for fintechs to reach customers through chartered banks. The direct effect is modest since the bill mandates no rule changes, but it sets up a friendlier policy conversation for the industry.

The bill asks regulators to study how partnerships can support new bank formation and community bank health, positioning banks as the permanent gateway for fintech services rather than opening a non-bank route. Any resulting rules would route consumer financial services through insured banks, reinforcing their gatekeeper role.
Credit unions get a separate study of their own fintech partnerships, which could help them offer modern digital products, though no relief is actually granted.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the Senate Banking Committee with a single cosponsor and no committee action. Similar study-only bills rarely move without committee leadership backing; its most likely path is to remain referred and expire at the end of the 119th Congress, though its substance could be folded into a larger banking package.
